variants.why: The original: a genitive plural, ‘of the Franceschi’ — the household of a Francesco. The apostrophe is the elided dei.
Not a variant at all: the Latin ablative the priest wrote. Franciscus de Franceschis. Mistaking case endings for spellings is the classic beginner's error.

variants.where: Western Istria — Seghetto and Svetvinčenat in 1945
variants.why: The settled Italian civil form, and what Carlo and Camillo put on their books. In the 1945 census the two households still writing it with a space are both in formerly Venetian territory — the spaced form survives only where Venice ruled, though the fused form is found there as well.

variants.where: Habsburg lands, Pazin county, Fiume — and Venetian Istria too
variants.why: Prefix fused into one word: an Austrian administrative habit, and the dominant form by 1945 on both sides of the old border. It is also the form that prevails in Trentino, Austrian until 1918. Note that after 1815 the whole peninsula was Austrian, so the habit had a century to spread everywhere.

variants.where: Split and Imotski · Italy · Corsica · the Americas
variants.why: Usually the prefix simply dropped — but in Dalmatia it was taken. The nobiliary *de* was removed from the Omiš–Imotski family by decree of the Napoleonic administration, which is why the descendants of a count are called Franceschi today. Not drift, and not a clerk: law.
German orthography reaching for the Italian c sound.
Slavic patronymic -ić written the Austrian way, -ich. Watch for this in reverse: an -ich name Italianised back to -i after 1920.
Italian schi is pronounced ‘ski’. An English-speaking clerk wrote what he heard. Thirteen of the seventeen people who carry this spelling worldwide are in South Africa.
The prefix restored onto a phonetic stem — a deliberate reclaiming rather than a clerk's error.

Listed on the old family site among the spellings. **This archive has not found it once** — not in a register, not in a census, not in a directory, in any of the eighteen towns swept. It looks like a mis-transcription of *dei Franceschi* with the -h dropped, which is a scribe's slip rather than a form the family used. Kept here because it was published for years and someone will come looking for it.

variants.where: Trentino, Friuli, Tuscany — and four people in this archive
variants.why: **Not a spelling of this name — a different surname that collides with it.** *Franceschini* is the Italian diminutive of *Francesco*, formed in its own right; *De Franceschi* is a genitive plural, «of the Franceschi». They meet in an index and nowhere else. Kept and listed because a search for one returns the other, and because this archive holds people under it — but **listed as adjacent, not as ours**.

census1945.source: Cadastre National de l'Istrie d'après le Recensement du 1er Octobre 1945, Institut Adriatique, Sušak 1946
census1945.note: Counts are families, not individuals. Compiled unofficially to support Yugoslavia's case at the Paris Peace Conference; the compilers omitted Muggia, Kastav, Rijeka and the hamlets toward Trieste, and Slavicised some names and toponyms.
census1945.finding: Of twelve settlements, ten use the fused Defranceschi and two the spaced De Franceschi. The fused form appears on both sides of the pre-1797 border — seventeen of the nineteen families in formerly Venetian territory use it. What is one-directional is the spaced form: it occurs only in former Venetian territory, never in the Habsburg interior. Not a border you can draw, but a survival you can point at.

Barban.why: Barban, in the Raša valley — this page had it at 44.97, eleven kilometres out to sea-ward of the village

Gračišće.why: Gračišće — Gallignana; this page had it seven kilometres north of itself

Pićan.why: Pićan — Pedena; this page had it nine kilometres north-east of itself

Čepić.why: **Ceppici di Pòrtole**, the hamlet by Oprtalj in the Poreč district — NOT the Čepić by Kršan in the east, which is forty kilometres away and is what every automatic lookup returns. The census names the district and the district settles it

Seghetto.why: A hamlet of **Umag**, which is the town the census gives; the point is Umag's ground, not a surveyed hamlet

census1945.mapnote: **Real ground, not a diagram.** The coast is Natural Earth's land, clipped to Istria and generalised; every settlement is at its own coordinates, and the four this page had in the wrong place are [corrected](/corrections/). The soft outlines are the **census's own districts** — Pula, Pazin, Poreč, Volosko-Opatija — drawn around the settlements this table names and nothing else. They are not surveyed district boundaries and **no pre-1797 frontier is drawn**, because the finding of this panel is that the spellings do not sort along one.

spellings_world.note: No entry exists for the spaced forms De Franceschi or de Franceski. **Re-queried 13 September 2026, and the per-country breakdown is added below** — the table above carries only the worldwide totals.

bycountry.heading: Where the two spellings actually are
bycountry.lead: Forebears gives a country breakdown that this archive had never taken down. Two spellings matter: the one the family mostly carries, and the one it carries here.
rows: **Italy 221** · United States 113 · France 93 · **Croatia 50** · Austria 43 · **Argentina 37** · Australia 27 · Canada 17 · Belgium 13 · Brazil 10. Most frequent in Italy and concentrated in **Trentino-Alto Adige**; **Croatia has the highest density** relative to population. Sixty-seven per cent are in Europe.

**South Africa 13** · Argentina 1 · Australia 1 · **Serbia 1** · **Slovenia 1**. Seventy-six per cent of everyone who spells it this way is South African, and within South Africa **100 per cent are in Gauteng**.

rows2.lab: Two countries this archive does not have
rows2.text:
Of the seventeen **Defranceski** in the world, one is in **Serbia** and one in **Slovenia**. Neither country appears anywhere on this site's map, in its register, or on its branch chart. One each is a household, not a line — but they are two doors nobody here has knocked on.

A third is in **Argentina**, which this archive has an open question about: Rotilio, eighth of the Eleven, is said to have gone to Buenos Aires with two daughters, and was searched for in September 2026 and not found. There is one person in Argentina spelling it the way this family spells it. **There are also 37 Argentine *Defranceschi*.**

This site says in three places that the thirteen are «in that city», meaning Johannesburg. The data says **Gauteng** — the province, which holds Johannesburg and Pretoria and much else. The city is an assumption laid over a provincial figure, and it is the sort of thing this archive corrects rather than keeps.

This site states, in two places, that the surname is «down to **about ten people in Croatia**». Forebears gives **fifty Defranceschi in Croatia**, and calls Croatia the country of **highest density** for the spelling.

The two numbers are not necessarily in conflict — «about ten» may be counting a line, or a village, or a single spelling, and the sources are of different kinds and dates. But the archive should know which it means, and at present it does not say. **Left standing, and flagged.**

bycountry.source: forebears.io, surname pages for Defranceschi and Defranceski, re-queried 13 September 2026. Forebears' national figures derive from electoral, telephone and census-derived datasets of varying dates, so they are a shape rather than a census.

zagreb.heading: A Zagreb school printed both spellings in the same line, in 1932
zagreb.lead: This archive has argued at length that the Croatian form of the name was not drift and not a clerk's ear, but a conversion — Austrian officials mistaking the Italian «de» for a claim of nobility, and families fusing the name rather than risk a fine. The argument has been made from the shape of the registers. Here is a document that simply prints the two forms as one name.
zagreb.quote: IIc razred. Razredni starješina Tiljak Zorka. Svršile su razred: 1. Blanda Marija · 2. Bužleta Ana · 3. Crnković Smiljana · 4. Defrančeski (Defranceschi) Milka · 5. Dugan Branka
zagreb.en: Class II c. Form mistress Zorka Tiljak. The following completed the year: … 4. Defrančeski (Defranceschi) Milka …
zagreb.why: The annual report of the State Second Girls' Grammar School in Zagreb for 1931–32, printing its pass list. One pupil's surname is given in the Croatian form with the Italian original in brackets after it — the school's own way of saying that these are the same name and the same family. That is the whole thesis of this archive's name page, set in type by a registrar in Zagreb who was not making an argument, only being accurate.
zagreb.more: She is not alone. The reports of the Zagreb state gymnasia between 1931 and 1940, digitised and searchable, carry a small cohort of the name in the schools of one city: Milka Defrančeski, who appears again in the First Girls' Grammar School list for 1932–33; Ljubica Defrančeski in the Third Girls' school for 1939–40; and, in the First Boys' Realgymnasium, Drago (also written Dragutin) Defrančeski and Milan Defrančeski, both across several years. Two of the girls and both boys are in Croatian orthography with the háček. Nothing here connects them to this family, and Zagreb is a long way from Gračišće. What they show is that by the 1930s the fused Croatian spelling was ordinary enough to fill a school register.
zagreb.source: Annual reports («Izvještaj za školsku godinu») of the State Second Girls' Realgymnasium, the State First Girls' Realgymnasium, the Third Girls' Realgymnasium and the State First Boys' Realgymnasium in Zagreb, 1931–1940, digitised and free on the Internet Archive; searched September 2026. Milka's entry is in the 1931–32 report of the Second Girls' school.

sarenjaci.heading: There was a word for people whose name was written both ways
sarenjaci.lead: On 1 March 1872 «Naša Sloga», the Croatian paper of Istria, printed a folk tale called «Šarenjaci» — the motley, the piebald. Daniela Simon's monograph on Istrian hybridity retells it, because it is where a word entered Croatian national politics that this archive's whole subject falls under.
sarenjaci.tale: A Croatian slave named Poštenjak — Honest-man — is pressed by a Turkish vizier to turn Muslim. He escapes it by telling the vizier a dream. In the dream, group after group of people file past, each dressed in a single colour and carrying a flag of that colour: gold for the Turks, white for the Christians, other colours for other faiths. Last of all comes a group in patched rags of every colour — «puno krpah svake barve» — with a flag of the same motley, poor and degraded. And the Prophet explains to him who they are: the people who in the course of their lives went over from one religion to another or from one people to another, and gave up their faith, or their people and their language.
sarenjaci.then: With that story the paper gave the Croatian national movement a name for the culturally mixed. «Mit der Bezeichnung Šarenjaci führte die ‹Naša Sloga› für die farbig gekleideten, verwahrlosten religiösen oder nationalen Konvertit*innen einen neuen Begriff in die politische Sprache der kroatischen Nationalkämpfer*innen ein. Er befeuerte eine aggressive Mobilisierung gegen die Betroffenen.» In the issues that followed, anyone held to be culturally mixed could be identified as a Šarenjak and called — Simon lists them — dull heads, empty hearts, snakes, a stench. The craftsmen and traders were only the spearhead. The men producing the paper were priests, which is why the story is a conversion story.
sarenjaci.us: Read that against this family. Friulian-Carnian in origin, weavers and then landholders, Italian in politics, living for three hundred years in a village whose speech a Polish dialectologist recorded as Croatian, and carrying a surname that the registers write «De Franceschi», «Defranceschi» and «Defrančeski» in the same generation. Miroslav Bertoša's seventy-six pages on them are titled «between ethos and ethnos». Šarenjaci is the word the other side had for exactly that position, and it was an insult. This archive has spent a lot of effort establishing that the fusion of the name was a bureaucratic accident rather than a choice. Both can be true at once: the spelling was forced on them, and the condition it left them in had a name that people shouted.
sarenjaci.caution: And the corrective, from the same book, which every family archive should have pinned above the desk. The Austrian census asked for «Umgangssprache», the language of daily use, and the revision sheets survive. «Die Bögen zur Revision zeigen, wie irreführend es war, von den jeweiligen Familiennamen auf die Umgangssprache oder gar Nationalität zu schließen» — the revision sheets show how misleading it was to infer from a surname the language of daily use, let alone nationality. At Kaldir, families with apparently Slavic names returned Italian; «selbst bei Familien mit demselben Nachnamen waren die angegebenen Sprachen unterschiedlich» — even families with the same surname gave different languages. The historian Vanni D'Alessio, who compared Istrian surnames against the registers, found that without the marriage, baptism and status animarum books the names were «als Quellen unbrauchbar», useless as sources — and that only the cross-check revealed the mixed marriages and local networks underneath. That is an argument for building a family from registers, which is what this archive does, and against reading anything at all off the spelling of a name, which is what most people do with theirs.
sarenjaci.source: Daniela Simon, «Die bedrohte Ordnung der Vielfalt. Kulturelle Hybridität in Istrien, 1870–1914», transcript Verlag, Bielefeld 2024, open access — the Šarenjaci tale at «Naša Sloga» 1 March 1872, the Kaldir revision sheets and Vanni D'Alessio's method as she reports them. Read in full text, September 2026.
sarenjaci.quote: Šarenjakom, koji nose u ustih medene rieči slobode, napredaka i prosvjete … a jesu tvoji najveći neprijatelji i zatiratelji najljući tvoje narodnosti.
sarenjaci.quote_en: Of the Šarenjaci, who carry in their mouths the honeyed words of freedom, progress and enlightenment — and are your greatest enemies and the bitterest destroyers of your nationality.
sarenjaci.quote_src: A letter from central Istria, «Naša Sloga», 1 September 1873. Before the Diet elections of the 1870s the paper warned its readers against electing Šarenjaci among the electors; a letter from Žminj told them to stop oppressing the national Slavs; and the threats to «traitors to the people» multiplied.

inuse.heading: Defrančeski, in living use, in print
inuse.lead: This site is called The Defranceski, and it has argued that the Croatian spelling with the háček is a real thing and not a corruption. Here it is in print, three times, in the mouths of ordinary men.

rows.text: A collection taken among the workers of the arsenal at Pula and printed in «Pučki prijatelj»: «po 1 Liru: Baćac Antun, Benčić Josip, Defrančeski Antun, Ladavac Franjo, Funčić Mate, Leverić Josip, Lorencin Jakov pok. Ivana.» One lira each. Antun Defrančeski, arsenal worker, written the Croatian way among Croatian neighbours, in the first year of Italian rule.
«Sabrano u Ližnjanu kod Pule… po 2 L: Fedel Jože, Fedel Ante Antunov, Defrančeski Ante, Vojnić Mate, Grakalić Martin…» Ante Defrančeski of Ližnjan, two lire.

rows.lab: And earlier, in the political press
rows.text: «Naša sloga», 1 October 1879: «svećenika lažanski i galežanski glasovala su za slobodnjaka Defrančeski-ja» — the priests of Lažani and Galežana voted for the liberal Defrančeski. That is Carlo, in the election a Bakar paper reported the same summer, with his own name declined into Croatian grammar by the people opposing him.

inuse.what: So the fourth spelling is not a twentieth-century accident of emigration papers. Croatian speakers were writing this surname their own way, in print, by 1879, and were still doing it in 1919 and 1920 — before anyone in this family reached Germany or Australia. Carlo explained in 1876 why the name split into De Franceschi, Defranceschi and Franceschi: Austrian clerks read the «de» as a claim of nobility. This is the fourth branch of the same split, made not by clerks but by neighbours.
inuse.source_inuse: «Pučki prijatelj» (Krk) and «Naša sloga», from dnc.nsk.hr, searched September 2026. Note that the portal's index does not do substring matching: «defranceschi» returns forty-four pages that «franceschi» does not, so each spelling has to be searched separately.

living.heading: The names still living in these towns
living.lead:
Forebears publishes, for each settlement, the commonest family names in it with counts — a snapshot of 2014. This archive had never used them. Set beside the registers and the gravestones, they answer a question no register can: **who is still there.**

Four towns, and they do not say the same thing.

rows.lab: Gračišće — the graveyard and the village still agree
rows.text:
**Jugovac 489 · Šestan 316 · Pauro 234 · Marfan 132 · Bomeštar 41 · Kmet Jugovac Pascale 31 · Maurović 31 · Stifanich 31 · Buljan 20.** No Defranceschi.

**Marfan is fourth.** This archive already had it — «one of the surnames standing beside Defranceschi in the Gračišće ground», read off the cemetery stones, with the F. MARFAN stone beside the obelisk and Marfan monuments elsewhere in the same ground. A hundred and thirty-two people of that name still live in the village. The living population corroborates the graveyard.

rows.lab: Vodnjan — the town those households lived in is gone
rows.text:
**Hrelja 208 · Macan 146 · Šverko 110 · Drandić 96 · Vitasović 96 · Lukić 81 · Červar 80 · Bliznac 76 · Diminić 76 · Pereša 76.**

**Not one** of the families this archive read out of Vodnjan's own registers is among them — not Francin, Malusà, Vellico, Gorlato, Giachin, Ferrarese, Demarin, Biasiol, Damiani, Zanghirella, Codacovich, Moscheni, Forlani or Tromba. And no Defranceschi, where the 1945 cadastre counted twelve families of the name.

That is the **esodo** in a list: the departure of Istria's Italian-speaking population after 1945, and the resettlement after it, visible as an almost complete replacement of a town's family names inside one lifetime.

rows.lab: Svetvinčenat — and the historian of the town is one of its commonest names
rows.text:
**Buršić 162 · Peršić 97 · Butković 95 · Perković 92 · Vitasović 85 · Doblanović 76 · Smilović 57 · Ban 51 · Cetina 50 · Frančula 50.** No Franceschi of any spelling, in a parish that gave this archive 118 records between 1628 and 1887.

**Doblanović is sixth, with seventy-six people.** This site cites *Doblanović on Svetvinčenat* — his study of the town's conceptions and births, and his judgement, with Brhan's, that the town's De Franceschi are Carnian. The scholar who wrote the modern history of this village carries one of its oldest surviving surnames.

rows.lab: Cerovlje — the municipality Gologorica sits in
rows.text:
**Poldrugovac 73 · Mikuljan 56 · Dundara 53 · Pauletić 50 · Baf 46 · Bašić 45 · Dagostin 41 · Privrat 41 · Jurada 40 · Santaleza 38.** No Defranceschi — which this archive already believed of its own village.

Two of those names are in its papers. **Poldrugovac** is the commonest name in the municipality today, and a **Frančisča Poldrugovaz** stood godmother at Krbune in 1843, to a child of Mariana De Franceschi. **Santaleza** is tenth, and a **Mattio Santalezza** married **Ellena De Franceschi** at Svetvinčenat in September 1751 — a different town thirty kilometres away, which is a persistence of a surname and not, on this evidence, a movement of a family.

living.close: **What the method is worth.** It cannot find a De Franceschi — the name has left all four towns. What it does is test the *company*: the allied families this archive knows from stones, godparent lists and marriage entries, checked against who is still in the village. At Gračišće they are still there. At Vodnjan they are not. That difference is itself a finding, and it was free.
living.source: forebears.io settlement pages for Gračišće, Vodnjan, Svetvinčenat and Cerovlje, read 13 September 2026; counts are theirs and dated 2014. Each list is the ten commonest names only — an allied surname surviving at rank fifteen would not appear, so a blank here is weaker evidence than a match.

scope.heading: What counts as this name, and what only looks like it
scope.lead:
This archive is a study of a **name**, not of one family — so the question «is this our bloodline?» is the wrong one to ask while collecting and the right one only when claiming. But a study of a name still has to say where the name stops.

**It stops before the diminutive.** *De Franceschi* is a genitive plural — «of the Franceschi». *Franceschini*, *Franceschina*, *Franceschino*, *Franceschinelli* are diminutives of *Francesco*, formed separately and meaning something else. They are collected here, because a search for one returns the other and because telling them apart is itself a finding — but they are **adjacent**, and nothing in them counts toward this name.

adjacent.why: the Italian diminutive of Francesco, a surname in its own right
the same diminutive, feminine — and also a given name, and two ships
the same diminutive; Florentine, and in the Medici papers of 1348 and 1354
a double diminutive, further away again
the Venetian clipping of the diminutive

scope.held: Thirty-five people of the adjacent names have pages in this archive, most of them swept up by an Austrian harvest. **They keep their pages and they are marked** — deleting a person because the ruling went against their surname would be its own kind of dishonesty, and the next researcher needs to know they were looked at and set aside.
